courseTitle: SQL Server HA, Backup & Disaster Recovery

slots.practicalActivity: On your own instance, create a test database (or restore a copy of AdventureWorks2012), set it to FULL recovery, and confirm the recovery model via sys.databases. Design and document a full/differential/log backup schedule for it matching a stated 15-minute RPO, then take one full backup WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM and (if a certificate/TDE is available in your environment) one WITH ENCRYPTION, documenting why encryption wasn't available if it isn't.
slots.deliverable: A written backup schedule (full/diff/log cadence) matching a 15-minute RPO, plus at least one real BACKUP DATABASE statement executed with COMPRESSION and CHECKSUM, confirmed via the backup history in msdb.

slots.practicalActivity: Modify the previous slot's full backup to write to two separate disk locations (mirrored or additional TO DISK targets), then run RESTORE VERIFYONLY against the resulting backup file. Finally, build one SQL Server Agent job that automates the full backup on a schedule.
slots.deliverable: A verified (RESTORE VERIFYONLY passed) backup written to at least one additional location, plus one working, scheduled SQL Server Agent job that runs the backup automatically.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the backups from Chapter 1, restore the full backup WITH NORECOVERY to a differently-named test database, apply the differential backup WITH NORECOVERY, then apply log backups in sequence ending with WITH RECOVERY, STOPAT set to a timestamp a few minutes before your last log backup. Confirm via a row count or timestamp check that later transactions were correctly excluded.
slots.deliverable: A fully restored test database at a specific point in time, with a written note confirming which transactions were included vs. excluded based on the STOPAT value chosen.

slots.practicalActivity: Restore your test database's backup chain onto a second local named instance (simulating "a new server"), taking a tail-log backup first if the source database is still online. Then deliberately break a restore chain by skipping one log backup, and use the resulting error message to practice diagnosing exactly which backup is missing.
slots.deliverable: A database successfully restored to a different SQL Server instance, a captured tail-log backup, and a written diagnosis of one deliberately broken restore chain identifying the specific missing backup.

lessons.title: HA vs. DR, Revisited for On-Prem

slots.practicalActivity: For your own environment (or a small-business scenario you write up), classify three possible failures - a disk failure, a ransomware event, and a data-center power outage - as HA problems, DR problems, or both. Then calculate the real downtime budget in minutes/year for three SLA tiers (99%, 99.9%, 99.99%) using this lesson's uptime math.
slots.deliverable: A one-page HA-vs-DR classification table for 3 failure scenarios, plus a calculated downtime-minutes-per-year table for 99%/99.9%/99.99% SLAs.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a comparison table of Availability Groups, FCI, log shipping, and replication across RPO, RTO, cost/complexity, and distance tolerance. Then apply this lesson's decision framework to a scenario of your own design (pick specific RPO/RTO numbers and a specific distance between sites) and justify which technology you'd choose and why the others don't fit.
slots.deliverable: A completed 4-technology comparison table plus a written one-paragraph recommendation for your own stated scenario, naming the technology chosen and the two it ruled out.

lessons.title: Creating an Availability Group
lessons.chapterTitle: Always On Availability Groups, Deep Dive

slots.practicalActivity: On your own environment (two local named instances or two VMs if available), create the database mirroring endpoint on each instance, then run CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP for a test database with one synchronous-commit, automatic-failover replica. If only one instance is available, write out and review the exact CREATE ENDPOINT / CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP statements you would run against a second instance, annotating every clause.
slots.deliverable: Either a working AG with endpoint and one joined replica confirmed via sys.availability_replicas, or a fully annotated, syntactically correct AG-creation script ready to run against a second instance when available.

lessons.title: Listener Configuration
lessons.chapterTitle: Always On Availability Groups, Deep Dive

slots.practicalActivity: For your AG (or script) from the previous slot, work out what SYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT vs. ASYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT would mean given your specific replicas' distance and network. Then add (or script) an availability group listener with a named virtual network name and IP, and write down why applications should connect to the listener name instead of a server name.
slots.deliverable: A written sync/async decision for each replica in your design, plus a working or fully scripted ADD LISTENER statement with a named listener.

lessons.title: AG Troubleshooting
lessons.chapterTitle: Always On Availability Groups, Deep Dive

slots.practicalActivity: If you have a working AG, run a manual ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER and verify the new primary role via sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states; if not, write out the exact failover and verification commands. Either way, query sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states to check synchronization health, and list 3 specific symptoms (e.g., NOT SYNCHRONIZING, a growing redo queue) you'd check for when troubleshooting a lagging secondary.
slots.deliverable: Either an executed and verified failover test, or a fully scripted one, plus a written troubleshooting checklist of at least 3 AG health symptoms and the DMV query used to check each.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram a 2-node FCI with shared storage, labeling the active node, the passive node, the virtual network name, and the shared storage volume. Write a one-paragraph explanation of why an FCI's failover doesn't involve copying any data, unlike an Availability Group's.
slots.deliverable: A labeled FCI architecture diagram, plus a written explanation of the active/passive failover mechanism and why shared storage makes it fast.

slots.practicalActivity: Research and document the quorum model (e.g., Node Majority, Node and File Share Majority) appropriate for a 2-node FCI with a tiebreaker file share. Write out the high-level setup sequence (WSFC installation, cluster validation, shared storage presentation, SQL Server FCI setup) step by step, and apply the FCI-vs-AG decision framework to one scenario of your own design.
slots.deliverable: A written quorum-model recommendation with justification, a step-by-step FCI setup outline, and one worked FCI-vs-AG decision for a scenario you defined.

slots.practicalActivity: Configure real log shipping between two local databases (or two named instances): a backup job on the "primary" writing to a shared folder, a copy job, and a restore job on the "secondary" using WITH STANDBY so it stays queryable between restores. Check the log shipping monitor/alert job for the actual restore latency.
slots.deliverable: A working log shipping configuration with at least 2 successful log restores applied on the secondary, plus a screenshot or query result from the log shipping monitor showing current latency.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page comparison of database mirroring vs. the AG and log-shipping options covered earlier in this course, specifically addressing why mirroring is deprecated but might still be encountered on a legacy SQL Server 2008-2016 instance. List 2 realistic scenarios where log shipping (not an AG) is still the right choice today.
slots.deliverable: A written comparison note covering mirroring's legacy status and 2 justified real-world scenarios favoring log shipping over an AG.

slots.practicalActivity: On your own instance, set up a basic transactional replication topology against a small AdventureWorks2012 table (publisher = your instance, distributor = same instance for simplicity, subscriber = a second database or instance). Confirm the Log Reader Agent and Distribution Agent are both running, then make a change on the publisher and confirm it shows up on the subscriber.
slots.deliverable: A working transactional replication publication/subscription with one confirmed end-to-end replicated change, plus the Log Reader/Distribution Agent job status.

slots.practicalActivity: Open Replication Monitor against your previous slot's setup and record the current latency and undistributed commands count. Deliberately stop the Distribution Agent job, make 3 more changes on the publisher, and use Replication Monitor to diagnose the resulting backlog before restarting the agent and confirming it catches up.
slots.deliverable: A before/during/after Replication Monitor record showing a deliberately induced backlog and its resolution, with the undistributed-commands count at each stage.

lessons.title: RPO/RTO in a Real DR Plan

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page DR plan outline for your own practice environment covering this lesson's real components (scope, roles, procedures, communication, testing schedule). State a specific RPO and RTO for it, then map each number to the specific backup/HA/DR technology from this course that would actually deliver it.
slots.deliverable: A one-page DR plan outline with named components, plus a stated RPO/RTO pair mapped to the specific technology choices that satisfy each.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a command-level runbook (exact commands, file paths, verification steps, like this lesson's example) for recovering your previous slot's environment. Run a tabletop exercise by walking a classmate, or a written narrative, through it step by step, then add a geographic-distance note (network latency assumption) and a communication plan naming who gets notified and when.
slots.deliverable: A command-level runbook document with verification steps, a written record of a completed tabletop walkthrough, and a named communication/escalation list.

lessons.title: Capstone Kickoff: Design HA/DR for a Real Scenario

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce Bellhaven Freight Systems' starting point on your own instance: create a BellhavenOLTP-style test database in FULL recovery, then implement the backup schedule from this lesson adapted to your environment - a nightly full backup (COPY_ONLY if you'll add a secondary in the next slot), a differential every few hours, and a log backup matching a 5-minute RPO.
slots.deliverable: A working backup schedule (full/diff/log) implemented against your own test database, matching a stated 5-minute RPO, with at least one successful run of each backup type confirmed in msdb backup history.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 1: verify your backup chain is actually restorable before building any HA on top of it. Run RESTORE VERIFYONLY against each backup type, then do a real test restore of the full backup plus the differential plus at least 2 log backups onto a differently-named database.
slots.deliverable: A successful test restore of the full capstone backup chain onto a separate database, with RESTORE VERIFYONLY results and the final recovered row count confirmed.

slots.practicalActivity: Using whatever multi-instance capability you have (two local named instances, or two VMs), adapt this lesson's CREATE ENDPOINT / CREATE AVAILABILITY GROUP / ADD LISTENER sequence to build a 2-replica AG around your capstone database, with SYNCHRONOUS_COMMIT, AUTOMATIC failover between the two. If a second instance genuinely isn't available, write out the complete, correctly-parameterized script exactly as you would run it, annotating every clause.
slots.deliverable: Either a working 2-replica AG with a confirmed listener, or a complete, clause-annotated AG creation script ready to execute against a second instance.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 2: if your AG is live, confirm synchronization health via sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states and test that the listener name resolves and routes correctly from a client connection. If you only scripted the AG, trace through the script line by line and write down what you'd check in each DMV immediately after running it.
slots.deliverable: Either a confirmed-healthy, listener-reachable AG, or a written DMV verification checklist mapped line-by-line to your capstone AG script.

slots.practicalActivity: Run (or fully script) this lesson's planned manual failover: ALTER AVAILABILITY GROUP ... FAILOVER targeting your secondary replica, then check sys.dm_hadr_availability_replica_states and sys.dm_hadr_database_replica_states to confirm the role switched and both replicas show SYNCHRONIZED, and fail back to the original primary.
slots.deliverable: A logged before/after role-and-sync-state capture from a real or fully scripted planned failover and failback, confirming a clean round trip.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 3: time your planned failover (or use the lesson's documented 10-30 second range, if scripted only) against a stated local RTO target of 15 minutes, and write a one-paragraph verdict on whether the HA leg of your design actually meets that target, with evidence.
slots.deliverable: A written RTO verdict for the HA leg, citing either your own measured failover time or the lesson's documented range, against the 15-minute target.

slots.practicalActivity: Script (and run, if you built a 3rd asynchronous replica or can simulate unreachability) this lesson's forced-failover command, FORCE_FAILOVER_ALLOW_DATA_LOSS, against your most-distant replica. Work out how you would measure the real data-loss window in your own environment - comparing the last-known transaction time on the old primary against what's visible on the promoted replica.
slots.deliverable: A written or executed forced-failover procedure, plus a concrete, named method for measuring the real data-loss window against a stated RPO target.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone lab 4: compare your measured (or estimated) data-loss window from the previous slot against the 5-minute RPO target set earlier in this capstone, and write a one-paragraph verdict - met, missed, or "insufficient evidence to confirm" - citing the specific number or reasoning behind your answer.
slots.deliverable: A written RPO verdict for the DR leg of the design, with the specific measured or estimated data-loss window cited as evidence.

slots.practicalActivity: Write the full 4-section runbook from this lesson (trigger decision tree, the two procedures, verification checklist, communication/rollback) for your own capstone AG. Assemble the whole capstone - backup strategy, AG design, both failover tests, and the runbook - into one portfolio document, then write a 90-second spoken answer to "tell me about an HA/DR project you built" naming the specific RPO/RTO numbers and what your tests actually proved.
slots.deliverable: A complete 4-section runbook document for your own capstone environment, plus a portfolio write-up and a rehearsed 90-second interview answer citing specific tested RPO/RTO results.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can design, implement, and test a real on-prem SQL Server HA/DR solution - backup strategy, Availability Groups, failover clustering, log shipping, and replication - against a stated RPO/RTO, and document a runbook someone else could execute during a real incident.
